turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning, Mrs Keating? Sorry, we've run over a bit. Your daughter was at the desk a moment ago, just so you know.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, yes, that's me. She didn't need to come, I can speak for myself. I've been in a proper state about these turns, if I'm honest.

[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): She was quite firm about it. Said last Tuesday you were confused, you couldn't make a cup of tea and you didn't know the day, and the sweating's been a month. Wanted it on the notes.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): A month? No, and I wasn't confused. I knew it was Tuesday, and I did make the tea. I was sweaty and I had to sit down, that's all. She always makes it bigger.

[SEG0005] person_3 (NURSE): Come on through, I'll do your checks. Don't mind me. My sister's got me on a wild goose chase for biotin, for her hair of all things, and my youngest was coughing half the night so I'm a bit foggy.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. I don't take that. Can I ask the doctor a lot of questions? I write them down and then I go blank.
[SEG0007] person_3 (NURSE): Ask away. Right. Blood pressure 146 over 82, pulse 78, finger-prick glucose 4.1 millimoles. Sit yourself there, Dr Shah's next.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello Mrs Keating, I'm Dr Shah. Sorry about the wait. Reception have passed on your daughter's account, but I want it in your words. What brought you in?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): The mornings. I wake up drenched, sweating through my nightie, and I'm shaky, my hands won't do what I want. Two weeks, I'd say. Is it serious, am I going to pass out?

[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): So, sweating and shaking on waking. You're saying two weeks, your daughter told reception a month, so I'll put it as roughly two to four weeks and not dress it up as exact. Are you eating breakfast?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, no. I skip it. Just a mug of tea and I'm out the door. Is that stupid? Should I be eating? I keep picturing myself fainting on the bus.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): It can matter with your medication. You've got diabetes, yes? Tell me what you take.

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, type two, about twelve years now. Gliclazide, umm, eighty milligrams every morning, I think, little white tablets. And metforman, metformin, twice a day. Sorry, I muddle the name.
[SEG0014] person_3 (NURSE): For what it's worth, when she checked in she told me the metformin was a thousand milligrams twice a day. She didn't hesitate.

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Did I? Oh, err, I don't know then. I think the box says five hundred, or it might be the thousand. The evening one I miss, two or three nights a week, but the morning gliclazide I never skip, breakfast or not. Is that wrecking my kidneys, be honest?

[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me say that back: gliclazide eighty milligrams each morning, you think but you're not certain, and metformin twice a day with the dose not agreed, five hundred or a thousand, some evenings missed. We'll read the boxes rather than guess. Any chest pain with these morning spells?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None. If I had chest pain would that be a heart attack? My neighbour had one last year and I can't stop thinking about it.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain would need a proper look, but you haven't had any, so I'm not treating this as a heart attack. Any blurred vision?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either. Optician in the autumn said the eyes were fine. Does a hypo wreck your sight? And can I still drive, doctor?
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): One low sugar doesn't damage the eyes. If you're shaky, don't drive, and if it starts while you're driving, pull over. Any shortness of breath?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Stairs are all right. What if it happens in the night and I don't wake up? That's the bit that frightens me.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): The morning gliclazide has usually worn off by night, so that's less likely, though I hear you. Have you ever blacked out, actually lost consciousness?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. I'd know, wouldn't I? Oh, and my husband takes metformin as well, a thousand of his, but that's his diabetes, not mine. Don't write his down as mine.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): I won't. His tablets stay his. Any excessive thirst? With diabetes that can creep in.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Normal drinks. I googled thirst and diabetes and now I'm worse. Is it a bad sign if I'm not thirsty?
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not on its own. And are you passing a lot of urine, or up in the night for the loo?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either. I sleep right through. So what is the gliclazide doing to me, then? I need to understand it.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any tingling or numbness in the feet? Over the years diabetes can dull the nerves down there.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes, at night, a tingling, not every night, and it's not painful. Are the nerves dying? Am I going to end up losing a foot, tell me straight?

[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not saying the nerves are gone, and plenty of people tingle a bit and keep their feet. Looking at you now, you're dry, no sweat, hands are steady, no tremor. Pulse is regular.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm all right this minute and the mornings are the problem. Is it a hypo? Should I stop the gliclazide today? I don't want to do something daft.

[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): I think those morning sweats and shakes are most likely a hypo, a low blood sugar. The gliclazide pushes the pancreas to put out more insulin, and if you haven't eaten the sugar falls, so you sweat and shake. I'm not stopping it today, but I do want food in you before that tablet. I also can't fully rule out the sugars running high at other times, which is why a blood test still matters.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Food, then the tablet. What do I actually eat, toast? And if I start shaking on the bus, what do I do, step by step? Are you changing the dose? Please, I need it clear.

[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Toast or cereal is fine, anything with some carbohydrate. If you shake, sit down, take something sugary like sweets or a sugary drink, and don't drive. I'm not changing the dose today, but I'll book a blood test this week for your HbA1c and kidney function, and I'll see you in a fortnight with the results. Bring both tablet boxes next time, and if there's a proper confusion episode or someone can't rouse you, that's an ambulance rather than waiting for me.

spec.situation: Older diabetic on gliclazide and metformin with morning sweating and shakiness; skips breakfast; daughter reports confusion once; doctor reviews doses and plans a blood test.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Reported by staff via daughter, but patient denies confusion; not resolved.
